name: Anthropology of Human-Animal Relations
description: This course is designed to critically discuss the dynamic and multifaceted relationship that exists between humans and animals from a sociological/anthropological perspective. The central questions are: How do humans socially construct and attach meanings to their interaction with animals and how does Anthropocene-inspired ontologies and materialisations affect human-animal relationship? What space do animals occupy in human social and cultural world? How are animals perceived and represented in one's culture? And, how can humans and animals live together and share life? Lestel and Taylor (2013: 183) argue that 'to be human does not mean to have fled animality, but on the contrary to live within it and to let it live within us...a shared life implies becoming oneself while being other'. Specifically, living together and sharing life not only invites us to recognize the agency, subjectivity and rights of animals but also problematises our understandings/assumptions about what it means to be human. Using anthropological and sociological perspectives, this course broadly discusses the social, economic and emotional interdependencies between human beings and animals, most particularly in the Indian context.
